title.narrative: Maternal and Neonatal Implementation for Equitable Systems (MANIFEST)

description.narrative: Each year in Uganda, nearly 46,000 newborns and 6,000 women die from problems during pregnancy and childbirth. Many of these deaths could be prevented if women and newborns received all the health services they needed, and parents practiced good newborn care. |This project seeks to combine, and scale up approaches tested during two pilot projects that led to an increased demand for maternal health services and improved newborn care practices. The pilot projects included home visits to pregnant women and newborn babies by volunteer community health workers, vouchers for transport and services, and work to improve care in health facilities. The projects showed good results, but did not show how the work could continue beyond the project period or how it could be expanded beyond the pilot areas. This project will combine the approaches from the pilot projects. Families, communities and district health management teams will be more closely involved, and will explore ways to plan and pay for the work, so it can continue without outside support. Combinations of the strategies will be tested in five districts in Eastern Uganda. The project will help show how each strategy can improve health service use and promote simple practices to keep newborns healthy. |As a result of this work, there will be a measurable improvement in the health of mothers and newborns in project areas. Results will be shared to promote wider use of the approaches.|Recommendation Summary: A grant of £228,001 for a nine-month design phase is recommended. This is an exciting project that showed strong improvements in indicators associated with improved maternal and newborn health during a pilot phase. It will support a well-respected Ugandan organisation, Makerere University School of Public Health (MakSPH) to take these findings to the next level: refining the work to make it replicable and part of local health systems, introducing the project in new districts, and using the findings to promote expansion. However, the proposal is not sufficiently developed yet to merit a recommendation to fund the full amount requested. The recommendation is to support a 9-month design phase that allows for further consultation with government and other stakeholders. This will result in a more clearly thought out and well-budgeted plan for the implementation and dissemination stages, for Comic Relief to consider in 2012.
